_meta.description: Shipping order books by segment, and the defense shipbuilding build-out, with every figure carrying its basis and date. Written 2026-09-05.
_meta.why_this_exists: Two things the owner asked for on 2026-09-05: order books across shipping segments (bulk, LNG, VLCC and the rest) and the growth in shipbuilding for defense. They share a yard base — the same Korean, Japanese and European docks build both — so they sit together.
_meta.reading_rule: An order book as a percentage of the fleet is NOT a forecast of oversupply. It has to be read against fleet age, scrapping and how much of the existing fleet is trapped in the shadow trade. The tanker segment is the live example: record ordering and an effective supply growth under 3%.
_meta.verification: Order-book ratios from Clarksons Research as reported by BIMCO and gCaptain (Q1 2026 orderbook; H1 2026 contracting). Dry bulk from Breakwave/Xclusiv (H1 2026). Fleet age and demolitions from AXSMarine and World Ports Organization (Jan 2026). Shadow-fleet share from Kpler/Hellenic Shipping News (Q1 2026). Defense figures from company releases and Naval News as cited per row. Figures NOT independently recomputed; each is attributed.

orderbooks.basis: 191M CGT orderbook / existing fleet, end Q1 2026 — highest ratio since 2011
orderbooks.note: Newbuilding orders in H1 2026 rose 66% year on year to 42.95M CGT across 1,481 vessels (Clarksons).
Highest of any segment. Tied to the third LNG supply wave (Qatar North Field, US Gulf Coast) — see Gluts: the wave itself was deferred by the March 2026 strikes on Ras Laffan.
Not held in this book. Listed for contrast: the segment most exposed to a deglobalisation-driven trade slowdown is the one with the second-largest order book.

A historically under-ordered segment. Crude tanker orders tripled in Q1 2026. Read against age: nearly 20% of VLCCs are 20 years or older, and many of those are moving permanently into the shadow fleet.
Tankers were 32% of all H1 2026 orders — their largest share since 2017.
Greek owners led the acceleration. Still the lowest major segment.
Limited replacement tonnage — the tightest supply picture on this table.

fleet_context.note: Record high. More than 1,440 tankers are over 21 years old.
Lowest in at least a decade. Old ships that would have been scrapped are trading sanctioned barrels instead.
Tonnage that has left the compliant market and does not compete with modern ships for mainstream cargoes.
This is the reconciliation of a 22–30% order book with a tight market: age and shadow-fleet absorption offset most of the deliveries. Inference from the sources above, not a single published figure.

defense.framing: Defense shipbuilding is the clearest case in this book of demand arriving as POLICY rather than price. Backlogs are at records across every Western yard. Two watchouts stated up front: (1) a backlog is not cash — Fincantieri reported a record €74.2bn backlog in Q1 2026 and its shares fell roughly 40%; (2) the US legislative piece is NOT law — the SHIPS for America Act (S.1541 / H.R.3151) has sat in committee since April–May 2025. What exists is an executive order (2025-04-09) and a Maritime Action Plan (2026-02-13).

rows.event: US Navy issued two Requests for Information to South Korean yards — one for fleet replenishment tankers, one for destroyer-sized surface combatants — the first step toward ending an 80-year bar on foreign-built warships. Congress must still authorise a national-security waiver and appropriate funds.

Hanwha (Hanwha Ocean + Hanwha Systems) bought Philly Shipyard for $100M in 2024, has spent over $200M of a planned $5B, grown to 2,000+ workers, and won its first Navy contract. HD Hyundai Heavy is cooperating with HII; Samsung Heavy with GD NASSCO on the next-generation logistics ship.

SHIPS for America Act — introduced 2024-12-19, reintroduced as S.1541 / H.R.3151 in April–May 2025, referred to committee. NOT PASSED as of 2026-09-05. Executive order 'Restoring America's Maritime Dominance' 2025-04-09; Maritime Action Plan released 2026-02-13.

TKMS spun out of thyssenkrupp and listed in Frankfurt 2025-10 at ~€60/share (~€3.8bn); thyssenkrupp retains 51%. Order book a record €20.1bn at end-June 2026. Canada selected TKMS over Hanwha Ocean for its submarine programme in 2026-07. Six Type 212CD boats on order for Germany and Norway. MoU with Fincantieri on underwater systems 2026-09.

Fincantieri backlog €74.2bn — 8.1× FY2025 revenue — with €42.7bn firm across 94 vessels to 2036. Guidance raised. The shares fell ~40% around the Q1 2026 print: the market is discounting execution and cash conversion, not the order book.
Saab received Poland's order for three A26 submarines, ~SEK 47bn, deliveries to 2038. Kockums merged into a new Saab business area 'Naval' from 2026-04-01.
BAE Systems order backlog £83.6bn at end-2025 on £36.8bn intake; 2026 outlook raised on UK submarine and US munitions demand.

Japan's largest-ever defense export: Australia contracted three upgraded Mogami-class frigates (first of up to 11; programme up to A$20bn, first delivery 2029). Domestically MHI won three upgraded Mogami for ¥128.6bn (~$806M) with Japan Marine United as principal subcontractor; NEC, Mitsubishi Electric and Hitachi supply radar and systems. New Zealand talks opened. Record FY2026 defense budget.
Austal — US and Australian naval yard (Mobile, AL). Not yet reviewed in depth; listed as the small-cap exposure to both programmes.

glut_watch.note: Where this ties to the Gluts view: shipbuilding is a capacity industry with 3–4 year lags, which is exactly the shape that produces gluts. The signal to watch is not the order book alone but order book MINUS (scrapping candidates + shadow-fleet absorption). For yards, the risk runs the other way — record backlogs invite capacity additions, and Korean yards expanding into the US are adding docks at the top of the cycle.
indicators: orderbook % of fleet by segment, quarterly (Clarksons)
